newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament in second reading of 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament in second reading of 1997 budget.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Wednesday began the second reading of the 1997 national budget draft after committees had recommended a slight revenue and spending rise.

During three months of work the committees put forward a proposal to increase budget revenues and spending by 150 million zlotys to 115.3 billion and 127.5 billion zlotys respectively, the budgetary committee head Wieslawa Ziolkowska said.

"The budget deficit of 12.2 billion zlotys remains unchanged," Ziolkowska told deputies. The gap will be an equivalent of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), forecast to grow by more than 5.5 percent in 1997.
In 1996 the budget gap was 2.5 percent of GDP against a plan of 2.8 percent.

Budgetary spending could increase further by an equivalent of $235 million, if Poland gets loans from international institutions for programmes to reform its ailing health care system and coal-mining sectors, Ziolkowska said.

The budget's macroeconomic assumptions remain unchanged from what the government had put forward, with year-on-year inflation forecast to fall to 13 percent in December 1997 from 18.5 percent last year.

The committees have also decided to earmark 500 million zlotys more for health care, education, judicial system and defense mostly at the expense of funds initially destined for central administration.
The lower house of parliament, the Sejm, is likely to pass the budget draft later this week or at a session next week, with the ruling left-wing coalition holding a firm majority.
The Senate then has a month to propose its changes before President Aleksander Kwasniewski signs the draft into law.
The Sejm also began to discuss the central bank's monetary policy outline, which provides for increasing money supply by between 27.4 and 28.4 percent in 1997.

The outline -- which parliament passes each year but which is not binding for the central bank -- envisagesa policy of high real interest rates to keep fast growing credit in check and help curb inflation.

Ziolkowska said the monthly zloty devaluation, now at one percent, should amount to 0.7 percent on the average in 1997, while the average central bank's lombard and discount rates should be at 21.6 and 18.6 percent respectively.
The rates are now at 25 and 22 percent respectively.
Ziolkowska questioned the cabinet's assumptions that exports would grow by 15 percent in 1997, 5.5 points more than last year, while imports by 21 percent, seven points less.

"This assumption seems too optimistic," she said, adding the imports growth rate was likely to exceed that of exports much more, creating a trade deficit of $12.6 billion, compared with the estimated $8.3 billion last year.
Ziolkowska criticised the government for leaving too much funds as reserves at the disceretion of the finance minister.

Some opposition politicians have earlier said such policy was meant to enable the ruling coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party to direct funds to their electorates ahead of this year's parliamentary polls.
Providing too much direct and concealed subsidies for inefficient industries served the same purpose, they said.
